indicators.label: Global surface temperature, 2025
indicators.note: The consolidated figure WMO reports in State of the Global Climate 2025, drawn from a synthesis of eight to nine independent datasets rather than any single one. When WMO first confirmed the year on 14 January 2026 it gave 1.44 C plus or minus 0.13 C; the March report states about 1.43 C. 2025 came second or third depending on the dataset, and it did this during a La Nina, which normally cools the global average.

indicators.label: Warmest year on record
indicators.note: 2024 still holds the record. 2025 did not beat it. What matters more than the ranking is the block: 2015 to 2025 are the eleven warmest years in every one of the eight datasets WMO uses, and 2023, 2024 and 2025 are the top three in all of them.

indicators.label: Three-year average temperature, 2023-2025
indicators.note: Plus or minus 0.13 C. This is the first three-year stretch to average above 1.5 C. It is not a breach of the Paris Agreement, which is written about long-term warming measured over roughly twenty years, but it is the first time the shorter average has gone through the line.

indicators.label: Global surface temperature, GISTEMP
indicators.org: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies
indicators.note: NASA's own baseline is 1951-1980, not pre-industrial, so this number looks smaller than the others while describing the same planet. NASA ranks 2025 second in its record but calls it a statistical tie with 2023. The NASA indicator page was last updated on 21 January 2026.

indicators.label: Global surface temperature, HadCRUT5
indicators.org: Met Office Hadley Centre, UEA and NCAS
indicators.note: Plus or minus 0.09 C, range 1.32 to 1.49 C. Third warmest in this dataset, and the third calendar year above 1.4 C. The Met Office forecast this a year ahead with a central estimate of 1.41 C, which landed exactly. The chart series here is on the 1961-1990 baseline, where 2025 reads 1.19 C.

indicators.label: Global surface temperature, Berkeley Earth
indicators.note: Plus or minus 0.09 C, third warmest. Berkeley also reports that 9.1 per cent of Earth's surface had its locally warmest year ever, affecting roughly 770 million people, and that no region anywhere had a locally record cold year. Sixteen countries set national heat records, down sharply from 104 in 2024.

indicators.label: Global surface temperature, ERA5 reanalysis
indicators.note: ERA5 is a reanalysis, meaning a weather model fed every available observation to produce a gap-free global field, so it runs slightly warmer than the station-based records. Third warmest, 0.13 C below 2024 and just 0.01 C below 2023. The absolute global average was 14.97 C.

indicators.label: Global surface temperature, NOAAGlobalTemp
indicators.org: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
indicators.note: Third warmest since records begin in 1850, 0.12 C below 2024 and 0.02 C below 2023. Against NOAA's usual 20th-century baseline the same year reads 1.17 C. Land came second warmest, ocean third.

indicators.label: Human-caused warming, 2016-2025 average
indicators.org: Indicators of Global Climate Change (Forster et al.)
indicators.note: Observed warming for the same decade was 1.26 C, so essentially all of it is attributable to human activity. This is the number that tracks the Paris goal, because it strips out El Nino, volcanoes and year-to-year noise. For 2025 alone the human-caused figure is 1.37 C.

indicators.label: Current rate of human-caused warming
indicators.org: Indicators of Global Climate Change (Forster et al.)
indicators.note: Range 0.2 to 0.4 C per decade. This is the fastest rate in the instrumental record. At this pace the long-term average passes 1.5 C around the end of this decade.

indicators.label: CO2 at Mauna Loa, annual mean
indicators.note: The Keeling Curve site, running since 1958 when the annual mean was about 316 ppm. Mauna Loa reads a little above the global mean because it sits in the northern hemisphere where most emissions are.

indicators.label: CO2 at Mauna Loa, latest month
indicators.note: July 2025 was 427.87 ppm, so the year-on-year rise at this site is 1.25 ppm. Monthly values swing by several ppm through the year as northern forests leaf out and die back, which is why the annual mean is the number to compare.

indicators.label: CO2, global mean
indicators.note: Plus or minus 0.09 ppm, averaged across NOAA's global network of marine surface sites rather than one mountain. Pre-industrial was about 278 ppm, so this is roughly 53 per cent higher.

indicators.label: CO2 annual growth rate
indicators.note: Plus or minus 0.09 ppm. This is a sharp drop from 2024, which at 3.76 ppm was the largest annual jump in the whole record. The 2024 spike came from El Nino conditions, big wildfire years and weaker uptake by land plants; 2025's La Nina let the land sink recover. Emissions themselves did not fall.

indicators.label: CO2, WMO Global Atmosphere Watch
indicators.note: Plus or minus 0.2 ppm, 152 per cent of the pre-1750 level. WMO's network gives slightly different numbers from NOAA's because it uses a different set of stations. Bulletin No. 21 is still the most recent as of August 2026; No. 22 with 2025 data is expected in autumn.

indicators.label: Methane, global mean
indicators.note: Plus or minus 0.61 ppb, and about 166 per cent above pre-industrial. Methane traps far more heat per molecule than CO2 but breaks down in roughly a decade, so cutting it buys near-term relief. The rise slowed after the 2020-2022 surge but has not stopped.

indicators.label: Nitrous oxide, global mean
indicators.note: Plus or minus 0.11 ppb, about 25 per cent above pre-industrial. Mostly from nitrogen fertiliser and manure. It lasts over a century in the air and also damages the ozone layer. NOAA's global record for N2O starts in 2001.

indicators.label: NOAA Annual Greenhouse Gas Index
indicators.note: The heating effect of long-lived greenhouse gases is 54 per cent stronger than in 1990. Total radiative forcing is 3.539 W/m2, of which CO2 alone is 2.333, equivalent to 539 ppm of CO2 on its own. The page carries only 'Updated Fall 2025' with no exact day, and 2024 is still the last row as of 8 August 2026, so no 2025 value exists yet.

indicators.label: Fossil CO2 emissions
indicators.note: A record, up about 1.1 per cent on 2024, with coal, oil and gas all higher. First released at COP30 in November 2025 and published in full in Earth System Science Data in May 2026 by Friedlingstein and 149 co-authors.

indicators.label: Total CO2 emissions including land use
indicators.note: Fossil emissions rose but land-use emissions fell about 9.8 per cent to 4.1 GtCO2, so the total was roughly flat against 2024's 42.4 GtCO2. Flat is not falling. Concentrations keep climbing as long as emissions are anywhere above zero.

indicators.label: Remaining carbon budget for 1.5 C
indicators.note: For a 50 per cent chance of holding to 1.5 C. At 2025 emission rates that is about four years. The budgets for 1.7 C and 2 C are 525 and 1055 GtCO2. These are 50-50 odds, not safety margins.

indicators.label: Total greenhouse gas emissions
indicators.org: Indicators of Global Climate Change (Forster et al.)
indicators.note: Plus or minus 5.5. Made up of 38.6 GtCO2 fossil, 4.6 land use, 9.3 methane, 2.6 nitrous oxide and 1.7 fluorinated gases, all expressed as CO2 equivalent. The decade average for 2015-2024 is 54.6.

indicators.label: Global mean sea level rise since 1993
indicators.note: Plus or minus 4.0 mm, from the stitched satellite altimeter record that began with TOPEX/Poseidon in 1992. WMO's State of the Global Climate 2025 gives the same thing rounded as about 11 cm above the 1993 level.

indicators.label: Rate of sea level rise
indicators.note: Plus or minus 0.5 mm per year, against 3.64 plus or minus 0.25 mm per year measured since 1999. The rate was around 2 mm per year when the satellites started in 1993, so it has roughly doubled. Different groups quote somewhat different rates depending on the window and the processing; they agree the rise is accelerating. Data through August 2025.

indicators.label: Arctic sea ice minimum
indicators.org: National Snow and Ice Data Center
indicators.note: Tied tenth lowest in the 47-year satellite record, alongside 2008 and 2010. The striking fact is not the rank but the floor: the nineteen years from 2007 to 2025 are the nineteen lowest minima ever measured. The charted series is the September monthly mean, 4.75 million km2, which is a slightly different measure from the single-day minimum.

indicators.label: Arctic sea ice winter maximum
indicators.org: NASA and National Snow and Ice Data Center
indicators.note: A statistical tie with 2025's 14.31 million km2 for the lowest winter peak since satellites began in 1979, so two record-low winters back to back. About 1.3 million km2 below the 1981-2010 average, and the ice is thinner as well as smaller.

indicators.label: Antarctic sea ice minimum
indicators.org: National Snow and Ice Data Center
indicators.note: Sixteenth lowest in the 48-year record, a clear rebound after four extreme years, but still 260,000 km2 below the 1981-2010 average. Strong southerly winds spread the ice out in the Weddell Sea in January and February. Antarctic sea ice swings hugely year to year, so one near-average season does not undo the drop since 2016.

indicators.label: Ocean heat content, 0-2000 m
indicators.org: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
indicators.note: A record, and the fifth straight record year in the upper 700 m. Over 90 per cent of the extra energy trapped by greenhouse gases ends up here, which is why ocean heat is a cleaner warming signal than air temperature: it barely notices El Nino. WMO reports the rate of ocean warming more than doubled between 1960-2005 and 2005-2025. Value read from the NCEI yearly world-ocean file on 8 August 2026; NCEI refreshes it quarterly.

indicators.label: Earth's energy imbalance
indicators.org: Indicators of Global Climate Change (Forster et al.)
indicators.note: Range 0.82 to 1.25. This is the single most fundamental number in climate: how much more energy Earth absorbs from the Sun than it radiates back to space. It has more than doubled since 1976-1995. WMO's State of the Global Climate 2025 added it as a headline indicator for the first time and reported a record high in 2025. Satellite work on CERES data finds it rising about 0.45 W/m2 per decade over 2001-2024, faster than models predicted.

indicators.label: Global glacier mass loss
indicators.note: Plus or minus 16 Gt per year, from the first full community reconciliation of glacier measurements: 233 regional estimates from about 450 contributors in 35 teams. Loss sped up 36 per cent between the first and second halves of the period. Total loss over the 24 years was 6542 Gt, adding 18 mm to sea level. That is more than either ice sheet contributed.

indicators.label: Projected warming this century, current policies
indicators.note: With every national pledge fully delivered it comes down to 2.3 to 2.5 C. Of the apparent improvement on last year's report, 0.1 C is a change of method and another 0.1 C will be given back when the United States leaves the Paris Agreement, so the new pledges themselves moved very little. Note: this UNEP page blocked our fetcher with HTTP 403, so the figures come from search results rather than a page we loaded ourselves.

indicators.label: Chance of a year above 1.5 C before 2031
indicators.note: From the WMO Global Annual to Decadal Climate Update, which pools forecasts from 13 institutes. It also gives an 86 per cent chance that some year in 2026-2030 beats 2024 as the warmest on record, and predicts annual temperatures in the range 1.3 to 1.9 C. An El Nino is expected at the end of 2026, which raises the odds for 2027.
